articles.headline: Our Black Hills Trip.
articles.text:
Thursday morning at four o'clock we started on, with "Spearfish or bust" filling all our minds. From the South Moreau, about twenty miles towards the Belle Fourche is the only gumbo on the route. We got through without any difficulty, however, and camped on Indian creek for dinner.

Soon after starting, a dark cloud began coming up in the west, its toad stool shape and threatening look portending a hard storm. The first couriers came in the shape of huge hail stones, averaging larger than a hen's egg. These were quickly followed by a hurricane of wind, rain and hail that soaked us completely through and in spite of heavy double blankets the hailstones left innumerable black and blue spots wherever they could hit. They came so thick and fast that it was utterly impossible to count the number of times a person was hit. From the size of a hen's egg at first the hailstones dwindled in size to that of a pea. The storm lasted over an hour and was the hardest we ever experienced.

About five o'clock we saw the first signs of human beings, except the E6 and Macy's that we had seen since leaving the brick yard at Medora. Coming to the top of a butte the valley of the Belle Fourche lay below us covered with farm houses and several small towns. We reached the new town of DeMores at 5:30 and were welcomed by D. C. Baker, who has built a good building and stocked it abundantly with grocery and general goods. Messrs. Guild and Gallop, who came to the Hills by way of Medora expect to build a railraod from DeMores to the Hay creek coal mines and it undoubtedly has a good fighting chance to become one of the best towns near the Hills.

Starting on at 7 o'clock we reached Spearfish at 10:30 and putting up at the Spearfish House, enjoyed the luxury of a splendid spring bed. Mr. Rogers, the proprietor, is a very popular hotel man, and he has been forced to build so many additions that he can scarcely tell his original building.

The morning of the 4th of July, all Spearfish had on its holiday clothes and in spite of the inevitable rain-storm, the parade and celebration were great successes.

Under the able guidance of Dr. Louthan and Maj. Snyder, we took in the town and surrounding country and were more than delighted with what we saw. Spearfish is located at the base of the northern Black Hills, near the eastern end of Spearfish valley,--a picture of loveliness. The whole valley is the very best agricultural land and irrigating ditches of magnificent spring water run all over it. Spearfish itself is a beautiful town of about eight hundred inhabitants and is one of the liveliest in the Hills country. The merchants are a wide-awake, generous lot of men, alive to every interest of their town. It is supported largely by stockmen and farmers and is bound to grow with the development of the country.

The morning of the 5th we started for Deadwood in one of Mr. Spear's stages, driven by Hank Monk, a fit descendant of the original. We had the honor of a share of Hank's seat and found him a regular encyclopedia of information. The first part of the ride was over the same agricultural country for which the Hills are famous. Many gypsum beds were seen, practically valueless now, but with railroad facilities it will become a valuable export, for use as a fertilizer and to be manufactured into plaster of paris. Falsebottom is a curious freak of nature that we crossed midway on our ride. It is the wide channel of a river but contains not a drop of water. A few miles above, there is a strong current that sinks gradually into the sand, continues its course underground and "bobs up serenely from below" several miles farther down. Soon we are in the Hills proper and now it is almost a continuous ascent to Deadwood, eight miles distant. The road-bed is a remarkably good one, although winding along at the foot and on the sides of Hills from four to eight hundred feet high. Everywhere, covering the sides and summits of the Hills has grown a dense forest of pine, closely resembling the Norway species. It is rather harder, thus improving its building properties. Except for the brick buildings, every house in the Black Hills region is built from these pine forests. The deep red waters of the streams attracted our attention. The discoloration is caused by the pulverized quartz hammered into powder by the stamps of the immense Homestake mills and others. The Homestake controls the water right of the Hills virtually, conducting it for many miles over mountains and gulches, by a system of ditches and flumes that is a triumph of engineering skill. This water is conducted to other mills than those of the Homestake system and thus a large royalty is made by them.

The trip through the Hills was a jolly one, the echoes fairly shouting back the refrain to "Hark, I hear a voice, way up in the mountain top," and many other college songs. Rounding a bend, we came upon the first miners we had seen, three Chinamen sluicing, at which we afterwards learned that they made, "sometime six bittee, sometime dolllah hap, when dig like hellee." No sooner had we passed these bias-eyed sons of toil than another bend brought Deadwood, the metropolis of the Hills in view.

(To be continued.)
articles.summary: Packard's serialized account of a trip from Medora to Spearfish and Deadwood: a severe hailstorm, the new Black Hills town of DeMores, Spearfish's Fourth of July, and a stage ride to Deadwood.

articles.text: The Cow Boy is much pleased to note the general satisfaction its legislative nomination is giving in Billings county and the hearty endorsement with which the selection of L. N. Cary is meeting. The Cow Boy is in no sense a political paper although as all our readers know it would be Republican, were there any use in a territorial paper mixing in national politics. We are thus the freer about upholding the candidate of our choice. Long before we had any idea of starting a paper in Medora, we remember that in a conversation with Mr. Cary, he spoke with much intelligence of the magnitude of Dakota's stock interests and of the necessity of fostering such a profitable industry. This conversation was remembered when we first heard Mr. Cary's name mentioned as a candidate and we straightway came out for the man who will certainly do as much as any one we know to look after stock interests. Billings county, as well as the whole west Missouri country can depend upon having an able representative if we send Mr. Cary to the legislature. In view of these facts it behooves Billings county to rally round the Cary flag as one man. Billings, being the junior county, certainly has no right nor desire to dictate to its neighbors, nor in this case will we stand dictation. Our man is straight, honest, politically clean and competent and Billings county's two votes will cheerfully be cast for L. N. Cary.
articles.summary: Editorial backing L. N. Cary for the territorial legislature as the stockmen's candidate and pledging Billings county's two votes to him.

articles.headline: $100.00 REWARD.
articles.text:
$100.00 will be paid for the return to Week's ranche, Beaver creek, Montana, of the following stock:

1 bay horse, branded NC, A above, on left shoulder.

1 buckskin pony, branded AIG on right shoulder.

1 buckskin pony, left front foot crooked.

1 sorrel pony.

All the above have hair brand of artist's palette with W in the centre, on left flank. Three of the above had ropes on them. $20.00 reward will be paid for any information leading to their recovery.

Culbertson & Weeks, Keith, Dawson Co., Dak.
articles.summary: Culbertson & Weeks offer $100 for return of four horses and ponies missing from Week's ranch on Beaver Creek.

articles.headline: $50 Reward.
articles.text:
The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock or a proportionate reward will be paid for the return of any of them. The stock consists of the following horses:

One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder as advertised in our brand columns. Also one light sorrel pony, white legs and face and branded NC on left shoulder and triangle JP on right shoulder also as advertised in our brand columns.

Gregor Lang, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang offers $50 for the return of three mares and a pony.

The above reward will be paid for the return of the team of large gray horses, half Norman breed, weighing twelve and thirteen hundred pounds, stolen from Belfield, Billings Co., Dak., May 26. No brand on them when stolen.

A. Anderson, Belfield, Dak.
articles.summary: A. Anderson of Belfield offers $125 for a team of gray horses stolen May 26.

articles.text: The stockmen of Mason county, in Texas, have furnished 20,000 cattle to the spring drive at an average of $15 per head, making the handsome sum of $300,000.--[Colorado L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Mason County, Texas, supplied 20,000 cattle to the spring drive. (clipped item)

articles.text: The Missouri Pacific is now running its stock trains in seven sections almost daily. This means that about 4,000 head of cattle go north every evening, the value of which is not far from $125,000.--[Vinita (I. T.) Chieftain.
articles.summary: Missouri Pacific stock trains carry about 4,000 cattle north daily. (clipped item)

articles.text: An enormous ranch in Mexico has just been purchased for $1,000,000 by a syndicate of English and Scotch speculators, of whom Lord Tweedmouth is one. It extends over sixteen hundred square miles.--[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: British syndicate including Lord Tweedmouth buys a huge Mexican ranch. (clipped item)

articles.text: The Denver papers report sales of some Iowa and Missouri heifers, ones and twos, in that city at prices ranging from $30 to $35 per head. Of course they were well graded up, and their off-spring from good bulls, will be valuable.--[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Graded Iowa and Missouri heifers sell at Denver for $30-35. (clipped item)

articles.text: Wm. Blair, foreman of the Comanche Pool, came in yesterday, July 17th, with his face wreathed in smiles of satisfaction over the splendid outlook on the range. He says the calf crop is showing up equally as well as was ever anticipated, and that about 5,000 calves have been branded. Beeves are taking on fat rapidly, and the Pool will start a bunch of about 600 to Dodge City on the 31st inst.--[Barber Co. (Kan.) Index.
articles.summary: Comanche Pool reports a good calf crop in Kansas. (clipped item)

articles.text: According to the last census two-thirds of the 11,000,000 or more of horses in this country are used for industial purposes, and almost 4,000,000, are employed almost solely to increase the enjoyment of the people. On an average of $250 each these driving horses have an aggregate value of $1,000,000,000--which is quite a sum.--[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Census figures on the number and value of American horses. (clipped item)

articles.text: The Swan Land and Cattle Company has purchased 450,000 acres of land from the Union Pacific Railroad Company, embracing all the alternate sections between Miser Station and a point near Fort Steele. This purchase will cover a large portion of the country now being ranged over by the company's cattle and give them a most magnificent property.--[Cheyenne L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Swan Land and Cattle Company buys 450,000 acres from the Union Pacific. (clipped item)

articles.text: A new route for trail cattle is being extensively used this year by herds going to New Mexico, Colorado and the northwestern ranges. Crossing Red river at Doan's, they are driven over the old trail to the North Fork, and thence up that stream and the Sweetwater to a point a little above Mobeetie, where they cross over the ridge to the Canadian, which they follow up to New Mexico. This route furnishes grass and water in abundance and is free from the heavy and exasperating levies of toll on cattle by the Indians.--[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: A new cattle-trail route from Doan's crossing toward New Mexico avoids Indian tolls. (clipped item)

articles.text: "Live stock shippers of the country are beginning to realize the fact that few of their number become rich men, and many are in the end impoverished, while with breeders the reverse is the case. No one save themselves seem responsible for this state of things, and if they desire to ruin themselves by overbidding for a chance to lose money on a producer's stock, they have a right to do so. Buying and shipping cattle is an industry closely allied to dealing in futures, and requires both caution and judgment beyond the possession of most men."--[Indian Chieftain.
articles.summary: Comment that cattle shippers, unlike breeders, rarely prosper. (clipped item)

articles.text: Another bunch of 3,000 head of Texas ones, to fours, mixed cattle, belonging to the Continental Cattle Company, en route to Montana, passed through Brush last Thursday. This makes 10,000 head of the same grade of cattle belonging to the company, that have passed through Brush within the week. The cattle did look well, considering the fact that they had very short grazing for the first three weeks' drive, and the long march, but they could not be favorably compared with those which rode in the cars from Texas in eight days.--[Brush Lariat.
articles.summary: Continental Cattle Company drives 10,000 Texas cattle through Brush, Colorado, toward Montana. (clipped item)

articles.text: The present season has been an uncommonly favorable one for the stockmen of Montana. The loss of the past winter, severe as it was supposed to be, is very small, and the crop of calves is a prolific one. The grass and range conditions at this time are excellent, and there is little to worry the cattle kings. But judging by what we were told yesterday by an intelligent stockman, some disappointment is likely to result from the general short-sightedness in not providing a sufficient number of bulls for the range. This is true of all our ranges, and the sooner the matter is remedied the better it will be for the stockmen. Every year the cattle business here is becoming more systematic in management, and this is one of the items that requires some attention at present.--[River Press.
articles.summary: Montana range conditions good but bulls are too few. (clipped item)

articles.text: The cattle and horse market is gradually advancing, and to-day Texas cattle and stock horses are bringing better figures than they did thirty days ago. She cattle are in demand, with a very small number offered. Large sales of one and two year old steers have been made in the past few days at good round figures, yearlings selling at from $16 to $17, and two year olds at $19 and $20. A few buyers have been holding off with the expectation that prices would decline, and must now pay higher prices. The depression in the money market is virtually at an end, and money is quite free. New buyers are arriving daily, and large amounts of money are constantly changing hands. Out of the 15,000 horses that have been brought to this market, not over 2,000 are left. Saddle horses are bringing $50 to $60 and stock horses from $27 to $35. About 1,300 horses have been sold since Saturday.--[Colorado L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Texas cattle and horse prices rising. (clipped item)

articles.text: Miss Maude Reed has been located for five years on the Little Dolores. Coming from Sweden a poor girl, Maude launched out into the far West and started with a few head of cattle, and by strict attention, economy, and braving all the hardships of a frontier life, she is to-day one of the shrewdest and ablest cattle owners in Mesa county. Many is the gallant cowboy that has doffed his sombrero and bestowed his most devoted attentions upon fair Maude, but up to the present writing she is yet heart whole. Miss Maude owns 140 head of good grade cattle and an excellent ranch worth a snug fortune. All this she has accumulated by her own exertions and good business management. Being a fine horsewoman, she superintends the round-up, cutting out and branding of her own cattle each year, markets her beef and attends to her bank account with as much shrewdness as any accomplished cattle dealer. Rumor had it that the fair queen was to bestow her heart and hand on a neighboring stockman this last week, but it must be only a rumor, as she still refuses to bow to cupid's yoke. We sincerely wish her well, with all the success this life affords, and warn all book agents, editors and sky-pilots that travel that way with the idea of picking up a fortune, that the lady is credited with being a capital shot, and an ardent admirer of woman's rights.--[Montrose, Colo., Enquirer.
articles.summary: Profile of Maude Reed, Swedish-born woman cattle owner in Mesa County, Colorado. (clipped item)

articles.text: A large force of teams and men is out putting up hay.
articles.summary: Hay-making under way with a large force of teams and men.

articles.text: Fred. Ertel and son Fritz, of Belfield, were in town Tuesday.
articles.summary: Fred Ertel and son Fritz of Belfield visited town.

articles.text: C. W. Sleeper started Monday for Duluth, on business for the company.
articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper left for Duluth on company business.

articles.text: Delegate John B. Raymond passed through Medora on his way west last evening.
articles.summary: Territorial Delegate John B. Raymond passed through Medora westbound.

articles.text: We are pleased to state that the team of mules stolen from A. von Steiger has been followed and recovered by him in Canada. Steiger is a stayer.
articles.summary: A. von Steiger tracked and recovered his stolen mule team in Canada.

articles.text: Mr. Garver, of Bismarck, a practical tin-smith, was here yesterday and this morning returned home. He will probably return soon and establish a tin-shop here.
articles.summary: Bismarck tinsmith Garver visited and may open a tin shop in Medora.

articles.text: Doc. Pennell returned last night from the Black Hills, where he had been to get twenty of Jones' Bros. mules. They are to be used on the Canadian Pacific road.
articles.summary: Doc Pennell returned from the Black Hills with twenty Jones Bros. mules for Canadian Pacific work.

articles.text: It is estimated that 2,000 cars of stock will be shipped from Beaver this fall. Telegraphic orders have been received to make arrangements for the shipment of this amount.
articles.summary: About 2,000 cars of stock expected to ship from Beaver this fall.

articles.text: On account of the success of previous dances, it has been decided to hold one tomorrow evening at the new hall. Every one is invited and an enjoyable time is a matter of course.
articles.summary: A dance announced for Friday evening at the new hall.

articles.text: Harry Tarbell and Chas. Eaton started for the Hills Monday, to look at a band of horses near Spearfish. If they come up to expectations they will be added to the Custer trail ranch band.
articles.summary: Harry Tarbell and Charles Eaton went to the Black Hills to inspect horses for the Custer Trail ranch.

articles.text: A Mr. Newton, arrived Monday from Ireland, having made the trip from there to Medora in just ten days. He is an acquaintance of Gregor Lang's and will spend some time at the Neimmela ranch.
articles.summary: Mr. Newton arrived from Ireland in ten days to stay at Gregor Lang's Neimmela ranch.

articles.text: Geo. Roderick and wife started for the Red river valley Tuesday morning. George has secured remunerative work for his teams there and will work during harvest, after which he will return here.
articles.summary: George Roderick and wife left to work teams in the Red River valley harvest.

articles.text: Chas. Jolly returned last Saturday from Sturgis, where he had gone to recover his horse. This horse strayed about two hundred and twenty-five miles and as Charlie says, would never have been recovered, had it not been for the Cow Boy.
articles.summary: Charles Jolly recovered a strayed horse at Sturgis, crediting the Cow Boy.

articles.text: About the quickest job on record of the kind, was that accomplished by Pat. O'Hara, yesterday. He began at eight o'clock to dig a well for the company at the stables and at three o'clock had a pump in, discharging the best water we have tasted for many a day.
articles.summary: Pat O'Hara dug a well with pump at the company stables in one day.

articles.text: Again has the sun risen and set on us. In other words, James Cook, Studebakers' agent for the northwest, has come and gone. "Jim" is one of the best men on the road, and what he doesn't know about making things agreeable, is a lost art. Come again and come often, Jim.
articles.summary: James Cook, Studebaker agent for the Northwest, visited Medora.

articles.text: One thousand head of cattle were shipped in Sunday morning by Ferris & Merrifield and driven to their range seven miles up the river. They were one's and two's, half steers and half heifers, and are said to be the best lot of cattle shipped west this year.
articles.summary: Ferris & Merrifield shipped in 1,000 head of yearlings and two-year-olds for their range seven miles up the river.

articles.text: The ice has been broken and Medora rejoices at the celebration of her first marriage ceremony. John Kiefer and Mary Jane Corcoran are the chief actors in this domestic drama, which we hope will run along smoothly and close with many recollections of a married life well and happily spent.
articles.summary: Medora's first marriage ceremony: John Kiefer and Mary Jane Corcoran.

articles.text: Mr. Hohnick, who is with Mr. Duryea's surveying party down the river, came in Sunday night for grub and mail. The party was sent out by the N. P. R. R. for the purpose of finding out what land it really owns and its prospective value. Considerable progress has been made, although the survey of the Bad Lands is attended with many difficulties.
articles.summary: Mr. Hohnick of Duryea's N.P.R.R. land survey party came in for supplies; the Badlands survey is progressing with difficulty.

articles.text: It seems that Mr. Dennis Bramble has again been getting in his funny work on the freighters. Mr. Ford went to Belfield and got the promise of $1.75 for freighting. Yesterday he loaded for $1.50, preferring this rate to lying idle as it was all Bramble would give, after the freighters reached Belfield. "Thus doth the busy little B---- improve each shining hour." It is well for him that he does, for he won't have many more to improve. We wish to prophecy again that in less than three weeks Bramble has handled his last pound of freight over the Northern Pacific.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy attacks Dennis Bramble for cutting freighters' rates at Belfield and predicts his freighting business will end within three weeks.

articles.text: Vic Smith suffered a peculiar mishap last Monday morning which might easily have terminated fatally. While out hunting, about nine miles northeast of here, he had just killed a deer when his attention was directed to a band of mountain sheep. Just as he started after these the ground gave way and horse and rider were tumbled into an underground wash-out twenty feet deep. Vic was pinned to the ground for several hours but at last succeeded in extricating himself and getting the horse on its feet. Tying his lariat around the barrel of his gun and standing on the horse's back he made a lucky throw and lodged the gun across the apex of the V-shaped hole at the top. A walk of nine miles brought him to Medora, where a party was made up that soon rescued the imprisoned horse.
articles.summary: Hunter Vic Smith and his horse fell into a 20-foot washout while hunting; he climbed out and a party from Medora rescued the horse.

articles.text: There are a few croakers in town who will be abated as nuisances if they don't stop their everlasting complaints. We wish it distinctly understood that there are no walls around the town and no string is tied to any resident. They certainly are not in earnest about their complaints or they would leave town. There is not a town on the Northern Pacific in which there is as much money circulating proportionately as in Medora and in which it is so easy to gain a living. The croakers know this but are contented to merely exist on the scraps that fall to their share. This gentry, happily few, had better get up and rustle, or immediately shake the dust of Medora from their feet.
articles.summary: Packard tells Medora's complainers to rustle or leave town.

articles.text: The freight house is very near completion and will be entirely finished inside of a week. The floor is nearly all laid, the siding is on, a pretty and durable cornice has been added and the shingling will be finished in about five days. That this building, which will cost $6,000 and the side-track, costing as much more, have been built for fun, is absurd. Just as soon as preliminary arrangements can be made, the matter will have been settled beyond all doubt, and Medora will be the only point to receive Black Hills rates. Not only this, but we are in a position to know whereof we speak, when we state that the stage line will be on at the same time. A proposition has been made by the Marquis de Mores and accepted to have a stage line running as soon as possible. This we know.
articles.summary: Medora's $6,000 freight house is nearly done; the paper says Medora will get Black Hills freight rates and that the Marquis de Mores's proposal for a stage line has been accepted.

U. S. Land Office, Bismarck, Dak., July 9, 1884.

Complaint having been entered at this office by John Weber against John Peehn for abandoning his homestead entry No. 1538, dated April 9, 1883, upon the SE 1/4, section 20, township 140, range 99, in Billings county, Dakota, with a view to the cancellation of said entry; the said parties are hereby summoned to appear at this office on the 21st day of August, 1884, at 10 o'clock A. M., to respond and furnish testimony concerning said alleged abandonment.

J. A. Rea, Register.

O. F. Davis, Att'y. for Contestant. 24-5t
articles.summary: Land office notice of John Weber's contest of John Peehn's Billings County homestead entry, hearing set for Aug. 21, 1884.
